newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela keeps South African markets on tenterhooks.
newsitem.headline: Mandela keeps South African markets on tenterhooks.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela had South African financial markets on tenterhooks on Thursday amid rumours of a possible relaxation of exchange controls when he addresses parliament on Friday.
Rumours are rife that Mandela will use the current window of opportunity provided by bullish markets to make a bold announcement on easing controls.
However, few market players are looking for a single "big bang" abolition of all restrictions since this would run counter to previously stated policy of a gradualist approach.
Some also say expectations of an announcement on Friday may be premature with the March 12 budget a more realistic date.

Mandela will open the 1997 session of parliament on Friday with a 45-minute address starting at 11 a.m. (0900 GMT) -- marking the start of a hectic period of keynote speeches and briefings by economic policy makers over the next six weeks.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, who briefed the cabinet on his 1997/98 budget on Wednesday, declined during a news conference afterwards to comment on the foreign exchange control rumours.

"I've seen some very interesting rumours in the market," Manuel said, referring to newspaper reports last month that Mandela's speech to parliament would herald a cabinet reshuffle in which Manuel would be shifted to the foreign ministry.
The reshuffle reports have been emphatically denied by Mandela and in the meantime one of the factors behind them, the steady downward trend of the rand, has been reversed.
Sources close to Mandela say his heir apparent, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, made a major input into the speech to be delivered on Friday.
Mandela is scheduled to step down at the next election in 1999 and in recent months has delegated more and more responsibilities to Mbeki.
Previous Mandela speeches opening parliamentary sessions have been long on general policy goals but short on specific initiatives or plans.
However, Tony Twine of Econometrix noted that after high-level ANC policy discussions last month Mbeki had signalled that notable speeches would be made during the opening weeks of parliament.

"So it looks as though it's going to be a slightly more important opening of parliament address than we've been used to. That's what the market is now tossing around like a dog plays with a chicken leg," Twine said.

He said no parliamentary opening speech had yet rivalled in importance that made by F.W. de Klerk in February 1990, when he declared that Mandela would be freed from jail, but that Mandela could change that record on Friday.
Next week cabinet ministers and Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals will brief parliamentary reporters.
